At 03:09:29 UTC the same user, via wsmprovhost.exe (WinRM) on nashua.dmevals.local, again opened lsass with 0x1F3FFF (Sysmon GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff). The only other LSASS opens in the window are svchost/wininit/csrss/AntimalwareConfig/CollectGuestLogs with 0x1000/0x1400/0x101001 masks, which are normal.

findings.title: No network sniffing observed; Azure Network Watcher agent install is benign platform activity
findings.summary: The only capture-capable component seen is Microsoft's Azure Network Watcher agent on scranton.dmevals.local. No tcpdump/windump/wireshark/rawcap execution and no pcap/sniff/promiscuous command lines or script blocks were observed.

findings.title: Attacker python.exe on nashua is a C2/exfil client, not a sniffer
findings.summary: On nashua.dmevals.local the attacker (user pbeesly) dropped C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe at 2020-05-02T03:10:23Z and launched it via PsExec64 from scranton.dmevals.local with plaintext credentials (\\NASHUA -u dmevals\pbeesly -p Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by -i 2 C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe), spawning it under C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe. The server answered 401 Unauthorized, i.e. the client was being induced to authenticate to an attacker-controlled listener — the classic forced-authentication pattern (SMB blocked, WebDAV fallback). The same destination 192.168.0.4 is contacted in the Windows window: on scranton.dmevals.local, powershell.exe running as DMEVALS\pbeesly connected outbound to 192.168.0.4:80 at 2020-05-02T03:08:47.769Z, followed by svchost.exe (LOCAL SERVICE) connections to 192.168.0.4:80 at 03:08:50.904Z, 03:08:50.988Z and 03:10:23.020-03:10:23.187Z — the WebDAV client stack (svchost/WebClient) authenticating to the remote host. This activity occurs on a host where pbeesly also ran a hidden PowerShell IEX stager, csc.exe compilation, sdclt.exe and sdelete64.exe anti-forensics, so the coercion is part of an active intrusion rather than benign file-share use. Note the Zeek and Windows windows do not overlap, so the two are correlated by host/address, not by time.

findings.title: DavSetCookie rundll32 invocations on scranton.dmevals.local are WebDAV client behaviour, not cookie theft

findings.summary: The windows.other System channel contains no DHCP-related event codes (1341/1342/1020/1063 absent from the 216-event code stack), no PowerShell script block referenced DHCP, and Sysmon event.code 3 destination ports contain no 67/68 traffic (top ports were 8443, 389, 88, 53, 135, 445). No Kerberos ticket-forging artefacts (no RC4 0x17 tickets, no krbtgt anomalies beyond normal machine-account TGT requests) were observed, so the ticket-theft family is supported by the credential-access precursor rather than by forged-ticket evidence.

findings.title: PowerShell Get-PrivateKeys exported all LocalMachine certificate private keys to .pfx files on SCRANTON, followed by anti-forensic cleanup
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, in the context of user pbeesly (SID S-1-5-21-1830255721-3727074217-2423397540-1107), a PowerShell script block named 'Get-PrivateKeys' was logged at 2020-05-02T03:04:56Z (script block 9d153741-75c3-4062-afe3-aeca0aee611b, Path C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\readme.ps1). It enumerates the entire cert:\LocalMachine store recursively and calls Export-PfxCertificate for every certificate with a thumbprint, writing each to $env:USERPROFILE\Downloads\<random>.pfx protected by the hardcoded password 'saribas'. One second later (03:04:57Z) Sysmon file-create event recorded C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx written by powershell.exe, confirming the export actually produced a private-key container on disk. At 03:08:51Z a second function 'Invoke-BeachCleanup' (script block 31f21f1d-9199-4d21-9ea8-c29b97841202, Path C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\psversion.ps1) deleted $env:USERPROFILE\Downloads\*.pfx, *.bmp, *.png and $env:APPDATA\OfficeSupplies.7z — i.e. the stolen certificate containers plus the staging artifacts. The same session shows prior collection/staging activity (Compress-Archive of documents/password-named files, a System.Drawing bitmap-decoded IEX payload from monkey.png, and HKCU Folder\shell\open\command DelegateExecute hijack setup that was later removed), so the certificate theft is part of a broader hands-on-keyboard intrusion. This is theft of authentication certificates/private keys (T1649) enabling on-host or domain authentication with the victim's certificates. The only other certificate-related registry hit (4657 on NASHUA for SystemCertificates\ROOT\Certificates\BE36A4562FB2EE05DBB3D32323ADF445084ED656, process C:\Windows\Sysmon.exe, SYSTEM) is a routine root-store blob update, and the 4768 TGT requests for pbeesly/SCRANTON$ are normal Kerberos logons; neither is attacker activity.

T1111.reason: No MFA/smart-card/token-provider interception artifacts. The Credential* registry hits are routine Credential Guard configuration (Enabled=0x00000000 by lsass.exe, Wininit event 14 'Credential Guard configuration: 0x0, 0') and standard CredentialEnrollmentManagerUserSvc service creation by services.exe.
